clinicalPearls: Autosomal dominant syndrome caused by germline loss-of-function variants in BAP1, a nuclear deubiquitinase and tumour suppressor; tumours arise after somatic loss of the remaining wild-type allele (two-hit mechanism).

Core tumour spectrum is uveal (ocular) melanoma, malignant mesothelioma, cutaneous melanoma and clear cell renal cell carcinoma; the clustering of these tumours within a family is a strong diagnostic clue.
BAP1-inactivated melanocytic tumours, typically multiple skin-coloured to reddish dome-shaped papules, are a cutaneous hallmark and are often the earliest manifestation.
Uveal melanoma associated with BAP1 loss carries a high risk of metastatic spread, particularly to the liver.
Mesothelioma in carriers is more often peritoneal, arises at a younger age with limited or absent asbestos exposure, and tends to follow a more indolent course than sporadic disease.
Loss of nuclear BAP1 expression on tumour immunohistochemistry is a useful marker and should prompt consideration of germline testing.
Recommended surveillance includes regular dilated ophthalmological examination, periodic whole-skin dermatological review and cross-sectional abdominal or renal imaging.
reference.pathophysiology: BAP1 (BRCA1-associated protein 1), located on the short arm of chromosome 3, encodes a nuclear deubiquitinating enzyme that removes ubiquitin from histone H2A and other substrates, acting alongside partners such as host cell factor 1 within the polycomb repressive deubiquitinase complex. Through this activity it regulates chromatin remodelling, transcription, the DNA double-strand break repair response, cell-cycle progression, cellular metabolism and regulated cell death, functioning as a tumour suppressor. Affected individuals inherit one loss-of-function allele, and malignant transformation characteristically follows somatic inactivation of the remaining wild-type allele in a Knudson two-hit fashion, abolishing nuclear BAP1 function within the tumour. Loss of deubiquitinase activity produces aberrant histone ubiquitination, impaired homologous-recombination repair, altered metabolism and disturbed differentiation of melanocytes, mesothelial cells and renal tubular epithelium, favouring the characteristic tumour spectrum. This same second-hit inactivation underlies the loss of nuclear BAP1 staining that can be detected by immunohistochemistry and used as a tissue marker.
additionalDifferentials: Familial atypical multiple mole melanoma syndrome (CDKN2A) for the cutaneous melanoma phenotype
Sporadic uveal melanoma without an underlying germline predisposition
Von Hippel-Lindau disease and other hereditary renal cell carcinoma syndromes
Familial or sporadic atypical Spitz tumours and multiple Spitz naevi
Other chromatin-remodelling or DNA-repair tumour predisposition syndromes
additionalInvestigations: Germline sequencing with deletion and duplication analysis of BAP1
BAP1 immunohistochemistry on tumour tissue showing loss of nuclear staining
Dilated fundoscopy and ocular imaging for uveal melanoma surveillance
Whole-skin examination with dermoscopy and biopsy of suspicious melanocytic lesions
Cross-sectional abdominal and renal imaging for renal cell carcinoma and peritoneal disease
Thoracic imaging where pleural mesothelioma is suspected
Histopathology of excised melanocytic tumours for BAP1-inactivated features
redFlags: New or enlarging pigmented ocular lesion or visual disturbance suggesting uveal melanoma
Unexplained ascites, abdominal distension or a pleural effusion suggesting mesothelioma
Haematuria or a renal mass indicating renal cell carcinoma
A rapidly changing, bleeding or ulcerating cutaneous pigmented lesion
reference.prognosis: Outcomes are variable and tumour-dependent: uveal and cutaneous melanoma carry significant metastatic potential, whereas BAP1-associated mesothelioma often behaves more indolently than sporadic disease. Early detection through lifelong multi-organ surveillance improves the prospect of cure.
pitfalls: Attributing multiple skin-coloured papules to benign naevi and overlooking BAP1-inactivated melanocytic tumours
Failing to consider a hereditary cause when mesothelioma occurs at a young age or without asbestos exposure
Assuming isolated tumours are sporadic and not eliciting the wider family cancer history
Not arranging coordinated lifelong multi-organ surveillance once the diagnosis is established
references: Clinical genetics and hereditary cancer references
management: There is no treatment for the underlying germline BAP1 defect itself; management centres on early detection and standard oncological treatment of each tumour as it arises
Localised renal cell carcinoma is managed with surgical resection, favouring nephron sparing surgery given the tendency to multifocal and bilateral disease over time

Advanced or metastatic renal cell carcinoma follows standard clear cell RCC systemic therapy pathways; note that BAP1 mutation carriers on VEGF targeted therapy have shown shorter progression free and overall survival, though no BAP1 specific regimen is defined
Localised uveal melanoma is managed with eye preserving therapy such as plaque brachytherapy or other radiotherapy, or enucleation for larger tumours, with surveillance for hepatic metastasis

Suspicious pigmented lesions or the syndrome's characteristic melanocytic papules are managed by excisional biopsy; confirmed cutaneous melanoma follows standard melanoma staging and treatment, including immunotherapy for advanced disease
Malignant mesothelioma is managed with surgical debulking or cytoreduction where feasible for localised or peritoneal disease, combined with systemic therapy
Advanced mesothelioma is treated with an antifolate-platinum doublet with or without an anti-angiogenic agent, or immunotherapy based regimens
Surgery is the primary curative approach whenever disease is localised across all tumour types in the syndrome
Systemic therapy is reserved for locally advanced, unresectable, or metastatic disease within each tumour type, following that cancer's standard regimen classes

Lifelong coordinated multi organ surveillance is recommended for confirmed carriers, including regular dilated ophthalmological exam and ocular imaging, periodic whole skin dermatological exam with dermoscopy, and periodic cross sectional abdominal or renal imaging
Maintain clinical vigilance for symptoms suggesting peritoneal or pleural mesothelioma such as unexplained ascites, abdominal distension, or pleural effusion
Loss of nuclear BAP1 expression on tumour immunohistochemistry should prompt discussion of germline testing
Refer to clinical genetics for germline BAP1 testing and cascade testing of at risk relatives when the diagnostic pattern is recognised or immunohistochemistry shows loss of nuclear BAP1 staining
Refer to ocular oncology, thoracic or peritoneal surgical oncology, or urological oncology as appropriate for suspected organ specific disease in a carrier
